statement: Let $f$ be an endomorphism of a [finite-dimensional vector space](c:finite-dimensional-vector-space) over a [perfect field](c:perfect-field). If $f = n_1 + s_1 = n_2 + s_2$ with $n_i$ [nilpotent](c:nilpotent-endomorphism), $s_i$ [semisimple](c:semisimple-endomorphism) and $n_i s_i = s_i n_i$, then $n_1 = n_2$ and $s_1 = s_2$.

hypotheses.text: The space $V$ is finite dimensional over a [perfect field](c:perfect-field) $K$.
The endomorphisms $n_1$ and $n_2$ are [nilpotent](c:nilpotent-endomorphism).
The endomorphisms $s_1$ and $s_2$ are [semisimple](c:semisimple-endomorphism).
Each pair commutes: $n_1 s_1 = s_1 n_1$ and $n_2 s_2 = s_2 n_2$.
The sums agree: $n_1 + s_1 = n_2 + s_2$.

proofs.name: Comparison with the polynomial decomposition
proofs.slogan: Compare both decompositions with the one whose parts are polynomials in $f$, then use that a nilpotent semisimple endomorphism is zero.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The proof shows that every decomposition has the same semisimple part $s_0$, the one that is a polynomial in $f$.

roles.why: Over a [perfect field](c:perfect-field) the existence theorem gives parts that are polynomials in $f$, and commuting semisimple maps have a semisimple difference.
Nilpotence of $n$ and $n_0$ makes their difference nilpotent.
Semisimplicity of $s$ and $s_0$ makes their difference semisimple.
Each $n_i$ commutes with $s_i$, hence with $f$, hence with every polynomial in $f$.
The equal sums say that both decompositions add up to the same map $f$.

steps.slogan: Take the decomposition of $f$ whose parts are polynomials in $f$.
steps.detail: The existence theorem over the [perfect field](c:perfect-field) gives $f = n_0 + s_0$ with $n_0$ [nilpotent](c:nilpotent-endomorphism), $s_0$ [semisimple](c:semisimple-endomorphism), and both $n_0$ and $s_0$ polynomials in $f$. It remains to show that $s_1 = s_0 = s_2$.

steps.slogan: Show that each given decomposition commutes with $n_0$ and $s_0$.
steps.detail: Let $(n, s)$ be $(n_1, s_1)$ or $(n_2, s_2)$. Since $n$ commutes with $s$ and with itself, it commutes with $f = n + s$, and likewise $s$ commutes with $f$. A polynomial in $f$ commutes with everything that commutes with $f$, so $n$ and $s$ commute with $n_0$ and $s_0$.

steps.slogan: Show that the difference $s - s_0$ is nilpotent.
steps.detail: From $n + s = f = n_0 + s_0$ we get $s - s_0 = n_0 - n$. The maps $n_0$ and $n$ are nilpotent and commute by the previous step, so their difference is nilpotent by the binomial expansion.

steps.slogan: Show that the difference $s - s_0$ is semisimple.
steps.detail: The maps $s$ and $s_0$ are semisimple and commute. Over a perfect field the algebra they generate is a quotient of a product of separable field extensions, so every element of it, including $s - s_0$, is semisimple.

steps.slogan: Force $s = s_0$ because $s - s_0$ is both nilpotent and semisimple.
steps.detail: A semisimple map has a squarefree minimal polynomial and a nilpotent map has minimal polynomial $X^k$, so the minimal polynomial of $s - s_0$ is $X$ and $s - s_0 = 0$. Hence $s_1 = s_0 = s_2$, and $n_i = f - s_i$ gives $n_1 = n_2$.

concepts.c:finite-dimensional-vector-space: Finite dimension gives minimal polynomials and the existence theorem.
concepts.c:perfect-field: Perfect fields make squarefree polynomials separable, so semisimple parts are polynomials in $f$.
concepts.c:nilpotent-endomorphism: Nilpotent maps form the first part of each decomposition.
concepts.c:semisimple-endomorphism: Semisimple maps form the second part and have squarefree minimal polynomial.

source.note: mathlib takes exists_isNilpotent_isSemisimple for $f$, shows that $s - s_0$ is nilpotent (commute_of_mem_adjoin_singleton_of_commute, Commute.isNilpotent_sub) and semisimple (IsSemisimple.sub_of_commute), then applies eq_zero_of_isNilpotent_isSemisimple.

statement: A [morphism of schemes](c:morphism-of-schemes) $f\colon X \to Y$ is [universally closed](c:universally-closed) if and only if it is [quasi-compact](c:quasi-compact) and every square $\operatorname{Spec} K \to X$, $\operatorname{Spec} R \to Y$, with $R$ a [valuation ring](c:valuation-ring) of fraction field $K$, has a lift $\operatorname{Spec} R \to X$.

hypotheses.text: The map $f\colon X \to Y$ is a [morphism of schemes](c:morphism-of-schemes).

conclusion: The morphism $f$ is universally closed exactly when it is quasi-compact and has the lifting property for valuation rings.

proofs.name: Universal specialization
proofs.slogan: Show that universally closed means quasi-compact and universally specializing, then match universal specialization with lifting along valuation rings.
proofs.scope: Both directions of the equivalence, for arbitrary schemes without noetherian hypotheses. The separatedness half of the valuative criterion is a different member of the family.

roles.why: Every step is about the single morphism $f$ of schemes and its base changes.

steps.slogan: Show that a universally closed morphism is quasi-compact.
steps.detail: Base change to $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)$ reduces to a scheme universally closed over a field. Base change to a polynomial ring with one variable per affine chart shows that finitely many charts already cover $X$. So fibers are compact, $f$ is a proper map, and preimages of compact sets are compact.

steps.slogan: Show that a quasi-compact map is universally closed exactly when it is universally specializing.
steps.detail: A closed map is specializing, and universal closedness passes to base changes. Conversely, a quasi-compact specializing map of schemes is closed, and quasi-compactness survives base change, so universally specializing gives universally closed.

steps.slogan: Turn a universally specializing map into lifts along valuation rings.
steps.detail: Given $\operatorname{Spec} K \to X$ and $\operatorname{Spec} R \to Y$, form $X_R = X \times_Y \operatorname{Spec} R$; the point $x$ over the generic point has residue field $K$. A specialization $x \rightsquigarrow x'$ over the closed point exists. The local ring of $\overline{\{x\}}$ at $x'$ is a local domain with fraction field $K$ dominating $R$, so it equals $R$: [valuation rings](c:valuation-ring) are maximal for domination.

steps.slogan: Turn lifts along valuation rings into universal specialization.
steps.detail: The lifting property is stable under base change. For a point $x'$ and a specialization $f(x') \rightsquigarrow y$, choose a valuation ring of $\kappa(x')$ that dominates the local ring of $\overline{\{f(x')\}}$ at $y$. A lift sends the closed point to a specialization of $x'$ over $y$.

steps.slogan: Combine the equivalences into the valuative criterion.
steps.detail: A universally closed $f$ is quasi-compact by the first step. For quasi-compact $f$, being universally closed, universally specializing and having the lifting property are equivalent by the other steps.

concepts.c:morphism-of-schemes: The criterion is a statement about one morphism and its base changes.
concepts.c:universally-closed: This is the property that the criterion characterizes.
concepts.c:quasi-compact: Quasi-compactness is needed for closed to equal specializing.
concepts.c:valuation-ring: Valuation rings are maximal for domination, which produces the lifts.

source.note: mathlib rewrites with universallyClosed_eq_universallySpecializing and ValuativeCriterion.Existence.eq (Stacks 01KE); quasi-compactness comes from Scheme.Hom.isProperMap and compactSpace_of_universallyClosed (Stacks 04XU).

statement: Every finite simple [regular graph](c:regular-graph) of even degree $2k$ is an edge-disjoint union of $k$ [spanning](c:is-spanning-subgraph) 2-regular subgraphs, called 2-factors.

hypotheses.text: The graph $G$ is finite and simple, with vertex set $V$ and $|V| = n$.
The graph $G$ is [regular](c:regular-graph) of degree $2k$ with $k \ge 1$.

conclusion: The edges of $G$ split into $k$ classes, and each class is a spanning subgraph with every vertex of degree 2.

proofs.name: Euler orientation and matchings
proofs.slogan: Orient the edges along Euler circuits, split the bipartite double cover into perfect matchings, and read each matching as a 2-factor.
proofs.scope: The case $k \ge 1$; for $k = 0$ the graph has no edges. The theorem does not claim that the factors are connected.

roles.why: Simplicity excludes loops and double edges, so the matchings give genuine cycles of length at least 3.
Even degree $2k$ gives Euler circuits and a balanced orientation with in-degree and out-degree $k$.

steps.slogan: Orient the edges along Euler circuits of the components.
steps.detail: All degrees equal $2k$, which is even, so each component has an [Euler circuit](c:euler-circuit). Orient every edge along these circuits. Each passage through a vertex uses one incoming and one outgoing edge, so every vertex has in-degree $k$ and out-degree $k$.

steps.slogan: Build the bipartite double cover of the orientation.
steps.detail: Take two copies $V^+$ and $V^-$ of $V$ and join $u^+$ to $v^-$ when $u \to v$ is an arc. The result $H$ is a [bipartite graph](c:bipartite-graph) in which every vertex has degree $k$, and it has no multiple edge because each edge of $G$ has one orientation.

steps.slogan: Split the double cover into $k$ perfect matchings by Hall's theorem.
steps.detail: In a $k$-regular bipartite graph, a set $S \subseteq V^+$ sends $k|S|$ edges into $N(S)$, which can absorb only $k|N(S)|$, so $|N(S)| \ge |S|$. Hall's theorem gives a [perfect matching](c:perfect-matching). Removing it leaves a $(k-1)$-regular graph, so induction gives $k$ disjoint perfect matchings $M_1, \dots, M_k$.

steps.slogan: Read each perfect matching as a permutation of the vertices.
steps.detail: A matching $M_i$ is a bijection $\sigma_i\colon V \to V$ such that $v \to \sigma_i(v)$ is an arc. There are no loops, so $\sigma_i(v) \ne v$, and an edge has one orientation, so $\sigma_i(\sigma_i(v)) \ne v$. Hence every cycle of $\sigma_i$ has length at least 3.

steps.slogan: Turn each permutation into a 2-factor.
steps.detail: Let $F_i$ be the set of edges $\{v, \sigma_i(v)\}$. Each vertex $v$ lies in exactly the two edges $\{v, \sigma_i(v)\}$ and $\{\sigma_i^{-1}(v), v\}$, which differ because cycles have length at least 3. So $F_i$ is a [spanning subgraph](c:is-spanning-subgraph) in which every vertex has degree 2.

steps.slogan: Check that the $k$ factors are disjoint and use every edge.
steps.detail: The matchings $M_i$ are disjoint, so the arcs $v \to \sigma_i(v)$ are distinct, and each edge of $G$ carries one arc. Hence the $F_i$ are edge-disjoint. They hold $kn$ edges, and $G$ has $n \cdot 2k / 2 = kn$ edges, so they exhaust $G$.

concepts.c:regular-graph: Regularity of even degree makes the orientation balanced and the double cover regular.
concepts.c:is-spanning-subgraph: Each 2-factor is a spanning subgraph built from one matching.
concepts.c:euler-circuit: Euler circuits give an orientation with equal in-degree and out-degree.
concepts.c:bipartite-graph: The double cover is bipartite, so Hall's theorem applies.
concepts.c:perfect-matching: Perfect matchings of the cover become the permutations that define the 2-factors.

source.note: Petersen's proof (J. Petersen, Die Theorie der regulaeren graphs, Acta Mathematica 15 (1891), 193-220) in the form taught in graph theory texts: Euler tour, bipartite double cover, Hall's theorem.

statement: For all [real numbers](c:real-number) $a$ and $b$, $2ab \le a^2 + b^2$. Hence for $x, y \ge 0$ the geometric mean is at most the arithmetic mean: $\sqrt{xy} \le (x + y)/2$.

hypotheses.text: The numbers $a$ and $b$ are real, or more generally lie in a linearly [ordered ring](c:ordered-ring).
For the mean form, the numbers $x$ and $y$ are nonnegative.

conclusion: $2ab \le a^2 + b^2$, and $\sqrt{xy} \le (x + y)/2$ for $x, y \ge 0$.

formal.difference: The declaration proves only the squared form $2ab \le a^2 + b^2$, in any linearly ordered commutative semiring with the listed order axioms. The square-root form follows by substituting $a = \sqrt{x}$ and $b = \sqrt{y}$.

proofs.name: Rearrangement of the ordered pair
proofs.slogan: Order the pair, compare the two pairings of the smaller with the larger by rearrangement, and substitute square roots for the mean form.
proofs.scope: Both forms, for two terms; equality holds exactly when $a = b$. The $n$-term inequality has its own record.

roles.why: The order of an [ordered ring](c:ordered-ring) lets us name the smaller and larger of $a, b$ and compare pairings.
Nonnegativity makes the square roots $\sqrt{x}$ and $\sqrt{y}$ exist as real numbers.

steps.slogan: Name the smaller and the larger of $a$ and $b$.
steps.detail: Let $m = \min(a, b)$ and $M = \max(a, b)$, so $m \le M$. Because $\{m, M\} = \{a, b\}$, we have $mM = ab$ and $m^2 + M^2 = a^2 + b^2$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two pairings of $m$ and $M$ by rearrangement.
steps.detail: For $m \le M$, pairing the small with the small and the large with the large beats the crossed pairing: $mM + Mm \le mm + MM$. The gap is $m^2 + M^2 - 2mM = (M - m)^2$, which is nonnegative in an [ordered ring](c:ordered-ring).

steps.slogan: Rewrite the pairing inequality as $2ab \le a^2 + b^2$.
steps.detail: By the first step, $2mM \le m^2 + M^2$ is the inequality $2ab \le a^2 + b^2$. Equality holds iff $(M - m)^2 = 0$, that is iff $a = b$.

steps.slogan: Substitute square roots to reach the mean inequality.
steps.detail: For $x, y \ge 0$, put $a = \sqrt{x}$ and $b = \sqrt{y}$, which exist as [real numbers](c:real-number). Then $2\sqrt{xy} = 2ab \le a^2 + b^2 = x + y$. Divide by 2.

concepts.c:real-number: The inequality and the square roots live in the real numbers.
concepts.c:ordered-ring: The order makes squares nonnegative and gives the min and max.

source.note: mathlib orders the pair with min_le_max and applies mul_add_mul_le_mul_add_mul to (min, max) twice, then simplifies with fn_min_add_fn_max.

statement: Let $g \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ and let $\hat g$ be its [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform). If the [Gabor](c:gabor-frame) system $\{e^{2\pi i m x} g(x - n)\}_{m, n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is a Riesz basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, then $\int x^2 |g|^2\,dx = \infty$ or $\int \xi^2 |\hat g|^2\,d\xi = \infty$.

hypotheses.text: The window $g$ lies in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$.
The [Gabor](c:gabor-frame) system generated by $g$ at integer time and frequency shifts is a Riesz basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$.

conclusion: The window cannot be well localized in both time and frequency: $xg \notin L^2$ or $\xi \hat g \notin L^2$.

proofs.name: Zak transform and Heisenberg commutator
proofs.slogan: Assume both localization integrals are finite, orthonormalize by the Zak transform, and contradict the Heisenberg commutator relation.
proofs.scope: The unit lattice in one dimension, for Riesz bases. The proof is by contradiction; it assumes $xg \in L^2$ and $g' \in L^2$, and the second means $\xi \hat g \in L^2$.

roles.why: The window is in $L^2$, so its Zak transform is defined and unitary.
The Riesz basis property bounds the Zak transform away from zero and away from infinity.

steps.slogan: Assume that $xg$ and $g'$ lie in $L^2$ and take the Zak transform.
steps.detail: Let $Zg(x, \omega) = \sum_k g(x - k) e^{2\pi i k \omega}$ on $Q = [0,1)^2$; it is unitary from $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ onto $L^2(Q)$ and quasi-periodic in $x$. Then $\partial_x Zg = Z(g') \in L^2(Q)$ and $\partial_\omega Zg = 2\pi i\,(x\,Zg - Z(xg)) \in L^2(Q)$, so $Zg \in H^1$. The hypothesis on $g'$ is $\xi \hat g \in L^2$ by the [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform).

steps.slogan: Show that the Riesz basis property bounds $|Zg|$ away from zero.
steps.detail: With $g_{m,n}(x) = e^{2\pi i m x} g(x - n)$ we have $Zg_{m,n} = e^{2\pi i (m x - n \omega)} Zg$, and these exponentials form an orthonormal basis of $L^2(Q)$. So $\{g_{m,n}\}$ is a Riesz basis iff multiplication by $Zg$ is bounded and invertible, that is $A \le |Zg|^2 \le B$ almost everywhere with $A > 0$.

steps.slogan: Replace $g$ by $h$ with $Zh = Zg / |Zg|$.
steps.detail: As $|Zg| \ge \sqrt A$ and $Zg \in H^1$, the quotient lies in $H^1$ by the chain rule and keeps the quasi-periodicity. Then $|Zh| = 1$, so $\{h_{m,n}\}$ is an [orthonormal basis](c:orthonormal-basis), and reversing the first step gives $xh \in L^2$ and $h' \in L^2$.

steps.slogan: Show that the basis coefficients of $Xh$ and $Dh$ have a conjugate symmetry.
steps.detail: Let $X$ be multiplication by $x$ and $D = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\frac{d}{dx}$. Then $X h_{m,n} = M_m T_n (Xh) + n\,h_{m,n}$ and $D h_{m,n} = M_m T_n (Dh) + m\,h_{m,n}$. Orthonormality kills the terms $n\,h_{m,n}$ and $m\,h_{m,n}$ in the pairing with $h$, so $\langle Xh, h_{m,n}\rangle = \overline{\langle Xh, h_{-m,-n}\rangle}$, and the same holds for $D$.

steps.slogan: Expand in the orthonormal basis to show that $\langle Xh, Dh\rangle$ is real.
steps.detail: Parseval gives $\langle Xh, Dh\rangle = \sum_{m,n} \langle Xh, h_{m,n}\rangle\,\overline{\langle Dh, h_{m,n}\rangle}$. The symmetry of the previous step maps the term $(m, n)$ to the conjugate of the term $(-m, -n)$, so the sum equals its conjugate. Hence $\langle Xh, Dh\rangle = \langle Dh, Xh\rangle$.

steps.slogan: Compute $\langle Xh, Dh\rangle - \langle Dh, Xh\rangle$ by parts and reach a contradiction.
steps.detail: Integration by parts gives $\langle Xh, Dh\rangle - \langle Dh, Xh\rangle = -\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int x\,(|h|^2)'\,dx = \frac{\|h\|^2}{2\pi i}$, since $x|h|^2 \in L^1$ vanishes at infinity. This is nonzero, against the previous step. So $xg \in L^2$ and $\xi \hat g \in L^2$ cannot both hold.

concepts.c:fourier-transform: The frequency localization $\xi \hat g \in L^2$ means $g' \in L^2$ through the transform.
concepts.c:gabor-frame: The Gabor system is the family of time-frequency shifts whose basis property is assumed.
concepts.c:orthonormal-basis: An orthonormal Gabor basis allows Parseval expansions and the symmetry argument.

source.note: Battle's commutator argument for orthonormal bases (G. Battle, Heisenberg proof of the Balian-Low theorem, Letters in Mathematical Physics 15 (1988), 175-177), with the Riesz case reduced to it by orthonormalizing the Zak transform.

statement: Assume the [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice). A closed ball $B$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ splits into finitely many disjoint pieces $P_1, \dots, P_r$ such that, for suitable isometries $g_i$ of $\mathbb{R}^3$, the sets $g_i(P_i)$ are disjoint and their union is two disjoint balls congruent to $B$.

hypotheses.text: The [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice) holds.
The ambient space is Euclidean 3-space and $B$ is a closed ball of positive radius.

conclusion: A finite partition of $B$ can be moved by isometries onto two disjoint balls, each congruent to $B$.

proofs.name: Free group of rotations
proofs.slogan: Find a free group of rotations, show that it is paradoxical, transfer the paradox to the sphere by choosing orbit representatives, and extend to the ball.
proofs.scope: The ball in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with rigid motions. The same holds in $\mathbb{R}^n$ for $n \ge 3$ and fails in dimensions 1 and 2, but this proof covers only $\mathbb{R}^3$.

roles.why: Choice picks one point from each orbit of the rotation group, which the pieces need.
Dimension 3 supplies the rotation group $SO(3)$ with a free subgroup, and the ball is a cone over the sphere.

steps.slogan: Find two rotations of $\mathbb{R}^3$ that generate a [free group](c:free-group) of rank 2.
steps.detail: Let $A$ and $B$ be the rotations by $\arccos(1/3)$ about the $z$-axis and the $x$-axis, elements of the [rotation group](c:special-orthogonal-group). For a reduced word $w$, suitably conjugated, $w(1,0,0) = (a, b\sqrt2, c)/3^k$ with integers $a, b, c$ and $3 \nmid b$, so $w \ne 1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the free group $F_2 = \langle a, b\rangle$ is paradoxical.
steps.detail: Let $W(x)$ be the reduced words that start with $x$. Then $F_2 = \{1\} \cup W(a) \cup W(a^{-1}) \cup W(b) \cup W(b^{-1})$, $F_2 = W(a) \cup a\,W(a^{-1})$ and $F_2 = W(b) \cup b\,W(b^{-1})$. So the disjoint sets $W(a) \cup W(a^{-1})$ and $W(b) \cup W(b^{-1})$ can each be moved by translations to cover $F_2$.

steps.slogan: Transfer the paradox to the sphere minus a countable set.
steps.detail: The group $G = \langle A, B\rangle$ is [countable](c:countable-set), so the set $D$ of points of $S^2$ fixed by a nontrivial element of $G$ is countable, and $G$ acts freely on $S^2 \setminus D$. By choice take one point from each [orbit](c:orbit) to form $M$. The sets $gM$ partition $S^2 \setminus D$, and step 2 makes them a [paradoxical decomposition](c:paradoxical-decomposition).

steps.slogan: Absorb the countable set $D$ by one extra rotation.
steps.detail: Only countably many angles $\theta$ fail to give a rotation $\rho$ about a fixed axis with $\rho^n(D) \cap D = \emptyset$ for all $n \ge 1$. Pick a good $\theta$. Then $\rho$ moves $D \cup \rho D \cup \rho^2 D \cup \cdots$ onto $\rho D \cup \rho^2 D \cup \cdots$, so $S^2$ is equidecomposable with $S^2 \setminus D$ and hence paradoxical.

steps.slogan: Take cones over the pieces to get the ball minus its center, then add the center.
steps.detail: Rotations fix the center, so the cone over each piece of $S^2$ gives a paradoxical decomposition of $B \setminus \{0\}$. A circle inside $B$ through the center, rotated by an irrational multiple of $2\pi$, absorbs the center in the same way as in step 4. So $B$ is paradoxical: it holds disjoint sets $A$ and $A'$ that are each equidecomposable with $B$.

steps.slogan: Read the paradox as a decomposition into two balls.
steps.detail: Let $B'$ be a translate of $B$ far from $B$. Then $A \cup A'$ is equidecomposable with $B \cup B'$, and $B \subseteq B \cup B'$. The Banach-Schroeder-Bernstein theorem for equidecomposability gives $B \sim B \cup B'$, so finitely many pieces of $B$ reassemble to two disjoint balls.

concepts.c:axiom-of-choice: Choice selects one point from each orbit, which builds the pieces.
concepts.c:free-group: A free group on two generators is the source of the paradoxical decomposition.
concepts.c:special-orthogonal-group: The rotations of space contain the free group and act on the sphere.
concepts.c:countable-set: A countable group fixes only countably many points of the sphere.
concepts.c:orbit: The pieces are built from one representative point of each orbit.
concepts.c:paradoxical-decomposition: The transfer step produces the paradoxical decomposition of the sphere.

source.note: The proof of Hausdorff and of Banach and Tarski (Fundamenta Mathematicae 6 (1924), 244-277) as presented in S. Wagon, The Banach-Tarski Paradox, Cambridge University Press, 1985, chapters 2 and 3.

statement: Let $r > 1$ be an [irrational number](c:irrational-number) and let $s$ satisfy $1/r + 1/s = 1$. The [floor](c:floor-function) sequences $\lfloor kr \rfloor$ and $\lfloor ks \rfloor$, for $k \ge 1$, have no common value, and together they take every positive integer.

hypotheses.text: The numbers satisfy $r > 1$ and $1/r + 1/s = 1$, so $s > 1$.
The number $r$ is [irrational](c:irrational-number).

conclusion: The two sets of values partition the set of positive integers.

proofs.name: Integers in short intervals
proofs.slogan: Test each integer by an integer in a short interval, show that exactly one of two intervals holds one, and use irrationality to match floor and ceiling.
proofs.scope: Rayleigh's theorem for irrational $r$. The first four steps hold for every $r > 1$ with the ceiling version $\lceil kr \rceil - 1$ of the second sequence, and irrationality removes the difference.

roles.why: The relation $1/r + 1/s = 1$ makes the two intervals fit together without overlap or gap.
Irrationality of $r$ makes $kr$ a non-integer, so floor and ceiling minus one agree.

steps.slogan: Express membership in a Beatty set as an integer in a short interval.
steps.detail: For an integer $j$, $j = \lfloor kr \rfloor$ iff $k \in [j/r, (j+1)/r)$, and $j = \lceil ms \rceil - 1$ iff $m \in (j/s, (j+1)/s]$. The endpoints satisfy $j/r + j/s = j$ and $(j+1)/r + (j+1)/s = j + 1$.

steps.slogan: Show that no integer $j$ lies in both sets.
steps.detail: If $k \in [j/r, (j+1)/r)$ and $m \in (j/s, (j+1)/s]$, adding gives $j < k + m < j + 1$ by the endpoint identities. No integer lies strictly between $j$ and $j + 1$.

steps.slogan: Show that no integer $j$ lies in neither set.
steps.detail: Suppose neither interval holds an integer. Take $k = \lceil (j+1)/r \rceil - 1$ and $m = \lfloor (j+1)/s \rfloor$. Then $k < j/r$ with $(j+1)/r \le k + 1$, and $m \le j/s$ with $(j+1)/s < m + 1$. Adding gives $j - 1 < k + m < j$, which is impossible.

steps.slogan: Restrict to the indices $k \ge 1$ and the positive integers $j$.
steps.detail: Since $r, s > 1$, for $k \ge 1$ both $\lfloor kr \rfloor \ge 1$ and $\lceil ks \rceil - 1 \ge 1$. If a value $j \ge 1$ comes from index $k$, then $kr \ge j > 0$ forces $k \ge 1$, and likewise for $s$. So $\{\lfloor kr \rfloor\}$ and $\{\lceil ks \rceil - 1\}$ partition the positive integers, also with $r$ and $s$ exchanged.

steps.slogan: Replace the ceiling version by the floor version using irrationality.
steps.detail: Because $r$ is irrational, $kr$ is not an integer for $k \ge 1$, so $\lceil kr \rceil - 1 = \lfloor kr \rfloor$. The exchanged partition of the previous step, $\{\lceil kr \rceil - 1\}$ with $\{\lfloor ks \rfloor\}$, is therefore the partition $\{\lfloor kr \rfloor\}$ with $\{\lfloor ks \rfloor\}$.

concepts.c:irrational-number: Irrationality of $r$ prevents $kr$ from being an integer.
concepts.c:floor-function: The sequences are floors, and the proof counts integers in intervals.

statement: Let $F_n$ be the [Fibonacci numbers](c:fibonacci-numbers) and let $\varphi = (1 + \sqrt5)/2$ be the [golden ratio](c:golden-ratio) and $\psi = (1 - \sqrt5)/2$ its conjugate. Then $F_n = (\varphi^n - \psi^n)/\sqrt5$ for every $n \ge 0$.

hypotheses.text: The sequence satisfies $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$ and $F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n$ for all $n \ge 0$.

proofs.name: Common recurrence and initial values
proofs.slogan: Show that both sides satisfy the same recurrence with the same first two values, so they agree for every $n$.
proofs.scope: All $n \ge 0$. The integer-index version for negative $n$ is a separate declaration and is not covered.

roles.why: The recurrence and the two starting values determine $F_n$ and give the comparison.

steps.slogan: Check that $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are roots of $x^2 = x + 1$.
steps.detail: We have $\varphi + \psi = 1$ and $\varphi\psi = -1$, so both are roots of $x^2 - x - 1$. Hence $\varphi^{n+2} = \varphi^{n+1} + \varphi^n$ and $\psi^{n+2} = \psi^{n+1} + \psi^n$ for every $n$.

steps.slogan: Show that $u_n = (\varphi^n - \psi^n)/\sqrt5$ satisfies the same recurrence.
steps.detail: The sequences that satisfy $u_{n+2} = u_{n+1} + u_n$ form a vector space, because the [linear recurrence](c:linear-recurrence) is linear. The geometric sequences $\varphi^n$ and $\psi^n$ are solutions, so their combination $u_n$ is a solution.

steps.slogan: Compute the first two values of $u_n$.
steps.detail: We get $u_0 = (1 - 1)/\sqrt5 = 0$ and $u_1 = (\varphi - \psi)/\sqrt5 = \sqrt5/\sqrt5 = 1$. These equal $F_0$ and $F_1$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two sequences by induction on $n$.
steps.detail: Assume $u_n = F_n$ and $u_{n+1} = F_{n+1}$. Then $u_{n+2} = u_{n+1} + u_n = F_{n+1} + F_n = F_{n+2}$. With the base cases of the previous step, $u_n = F_n$ for all $n \ge 0$.

concepts.c:fibonacci-numbers: These are the numbers whose closed form the formula gives.
concepts.c:golden-ratio: The golden ratio $\varphi$ is a root of the characteristic equation.
concepts.c:linear-recurrence: Linearity makes combinations of solutions again solutions.

source.note: mathlib shows that fib and the combination of geometric sequences both solve fibRec (fib_isSol_fibRec, geom_goldenRatio_isSol_fibRec, solSpace), then uses LinearRecurrence.eq_iff_eqOn_range_order.

statement: Let $f\colon X \to Y$ be a non-constant [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) map of [Riemann surfaces](c:riemann-surface) and $p \in X$. Then there are an integer $k \ge 1$ and charts centered at $p$ and at $f(p)$ in which $f$ reads $z \mapsto z^k$.

hypotheses.text: The spaces $X$ and $Y$ are [Riemann surfaces](c:riemann-surface), in particular $X$ is connected.
The map $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function).
The map $f$ is not constant.

conclusion: There are an integer $k \ge 1$ and centered charts at $p$ and $f(p)$ in which $f(z) = z^k$.

proofs.name: Root of the leading factor
proofs.slogan: Write $f$ in charts as $z^k h(z)$ with $h(0) \ne 0$, take a $k$-th root of $h$, and use $z\,h(z)^{1/k}$ as the new coordinate.
proofs.scope: Local statement at any point $p$. The integer $k$ is the [ramification index](c:ramification-index) of $f$ at $p$, and the map is locally $k$-to-one near $p$.

roles.why: Charts reduce the problem to a function on a disc, and connectedness lets the identity theorem act.
Holomorphy gives a power series and a holomorphic root.
Non-constancy rules out $F \equiv 0$ near $p$.

steps.slogan: Write $f$ in centered charts as a holomorphic function $F$ with $F(0) = 0$.
steps.detail: Choose centered charts $\varphi$ at $p$ and $\psi$ at $f(p)$, and shrink the first so that $f$ maps its domain into the second. Then $F = \psi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on a disc around $0$ with $F(0) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $F$ is not identically zero near $0$.
steps.detail: If $F \equiv 0$ near $0$, then $f$ equals the constant $f(p)$ on an open set. The identity theorem on the connected [Riemann surface](c:riemann-surface) $X$ then makes $f$ constant, against the hypothesis.

steps.slogan: Factor out the vanishing order: $F(z) = z^k h(z)$ with $h(0) \ne 0$.
steps.detail: The power series of $F$ at $0$ is nonzero and has no constant term. Let $k \ge 1$ be the first index with a nonzero coefficient. Then $F(z) = z^k h(z)$ with $h$ holomorphic and $h(0) \ne 0$.

steps.slogan: Choose a holomorphic $k$-th root $g$ of $h$ near $0$.
steps.detail: Since $h(0) \ne 0$, shrink the disc so that $h$ takes values in a disc that misses $0$. A branch of the $k$-th root is defined there, which gives a holomorphic $g$ with $g^k = h$ and $g(0) \ne 0$.

steps.slogan: Use $\zeta = z\,g(z)$ as a new centered coordinate.
steps.detail: We have $\zeta'(0) = g(0) \ne 0$, so by the inverse function theorem $\zeta$ is biholomorphic near $0$ and is a new chart centered at $p$. In it, $F = z^k g^k = \zeta^k$.

concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy gives power series expansions and holomorphic roots.
concepts.c:riemann-surface: Charts of a connected Riemann surface reduce the claim to a disc.
concepts.c:ramification-index: The exponent $k$ is the local degree of the map at $p$.

source.note: The standard local normal form proof, as in O. Forster, Lectures on Riemann Surfaces, Springer GTM 81, 1981, Theorem 2.1.

statement: Let $f$ be [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on $0 < |z - a| < r$ with an [essential singularity](c:essential-singularity) at $a$. Then for every $\rho \in (0, r)$ the set $f(\{0 < |z - a| < \rho\})$ is dense in $\mathbb{C}$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on a punctured disc around $a$.
The point $a$ is an [essential singularity](c:essential-singularity) of $f$: neither removable nor a pole.

conclusion: Near $a$, the values of $f$ come arbitrarily close to every complex number.

proofs.name: Reciprocal of a shifted function
proofs.slogan: Suppose a punctured neighborhood misses a disc, form the bounded reciprocal, remove its singularity, and show that $a$ is then removable or a pole.
proofs.scope: All $\rho \in (0, r)$ and all target values $w_0 \in \mathbb{C}$. Picard's great theorem strengthens the statement and is a separate result.

roles.why: Holomorphy makes $g = 1/(f - w_0)$ holomorphic and lets Riemann's theorem extend it.
The essential singularity contradicts the conclusion that $a$ is removable or a pole.

steps.slogan: Assume that a punctured neighborhood misses a disc around $w_0$.
steps.detail: Suppose that for some $\rho$ the image of $0 < |z - a| < \rho$ is not dense. Then there are $w_0 \in \mathbb{C}$ and $\delta > 0$ with $|f(z) - w_0| \ge \delta$ for all $z$ in that neighborhood.

steps.slogan: Form $g = 1/(f - w_0)$, which is holomorphic and bounded.
steps.detail: On the punctured neighborhood $f - w_0$ never vanishes, so $g = 1/(f - w_0)$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) there, and $|g| \le 1/\delta$.

steps.slogan: Extend $g$ holomorphically across $a$.
steps.detail: A holomorphic function that is bounded near an isolated singularity has a removable singularity, so $g$ extends to $a$. The extension is not identically zero, because $g$ has no zero on the punctured neighborhood.

steps.slogan: Split on whether $g(a)$ is zero.
steps.detail: If $g(a) \ne 0$, then $f = w_0 + 1/g$ is holomorphic near $a$. If $g(a) = 0$, then $g(z) = (z - a)^m u(z)$ with $m \ge 1$ and $u(a) \ne 0$, so $f = w_0 + (z - a)^{-m}/u(z)$ has finitely many negative terms in its [Laurent series](c:laurent-series) and a pole at $a$.

steps.slogan: Contradict the essential singularity.
steps.detail: In both cases $a$ is a removable singularity or a pole of $f$, which an [essential singularity](c:essential-singularity) is not. So no such $w_0$ and $\delta$ exist, and the image is dense.

concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy of the reciprocal allows Riemann's removable singularity theorem.
concepts.c:essential-singularity: The conclusion contradicts the type of singularity that is assumed.
concepts.c:laurent-series: The Laurent series shows finitely many negative terms, which means a pole.

source.note: The classical proof by contradiction with the reciprocal $1/(f - w_0)$, as in Ahlfors, Complex Analysis, and Conway, Functions of One Complex Variable.

statement: Let $\sum a_n$ and $\sum b_n$ be convergent [series](c:series) with sums $A$ and $B$, and let $c_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k b_{n-k}$. Then the Cesàro means $\frac{1}{N+1}(C_0 + \dots + C_N)$ of the partial sums $C_N = c_0 + \dots + c_N$ converge to $AB$.

hypotheses.text: The [series](c:series) $\sum a_n$ converges to $A$.
The [series](c:series) $\sum b_n$ converges to $B$.

proofs.name: Cesàro means of the convolution
proofs.slogan: Write the sum of partial sums of the product as a convolution of partial sums, split off the limits, and show that the error terms have mean zero.
proofs.scope: Cesàro's theorem on the Cauchy product, for complex terms. Cauchy's theorem for [absolutely convergent](c:absolute-convergence) series and Mertens' theorem give convergence of $\sum c_n$ itself and are other members of the family.

roles.why: Convergence of $\sum a_n$ makes $A_k - A$ a null sequence.
Convergence of $\sum b_n$ makes $B_k - B$ a null sequence.

steps.slogan: Express the sum of the partial sums of the product through the partial sums of the factors.
steps.detail: Let $A_k = a_0 + \dots + a_k$ and $B_k = b_0 + \dots + b_k$. A pair $(i, j)$ with $i + j \le N$ occurs in $A_k B_{N-k}$ for exactly $N + 1 - i - j$ values of $k$, and in $C_0 + \dots + C_N$ with the same multiplicity. So $C_0 + \dots + C_N = \sum_{k=0}^{N} A_k B_{N-k}$.

steps.slogan: Write $A_k = A + \alpha_k$ and $B_k = B + \beta_k$ with null sequences.
steps.detail: By hypothesis $\alpha_k \to 0$ and $\beta_k \to 0$. Expanding the product gives $\frac{1}{N+1}\sum_k A_k B_{N-k} = AB + \frac{B}{N+1}\sum_k \alpha_k + \frac{A}{N+1}\sum_k \beta_{N-k} + \frac{1}{N+1}\sum_k \alpha_k \beta_{N-k}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the mean of a null sequence is null.
steps.detail: Let $|\alpha_k| \le M$ and fix $\varepsilon > 0$. Choose $K$ with $|\alpha_k| < \varepsilon$ for $k \ge K$. Then $\big|\frac{1}{N+1}\sum_{k \le N} \alpha_k\big| \le \frac{KM}{N+1} + \varepsilon$, which is below $2\varepsilon$ for large $N$. The same holds for $\beta$, so both linear terms tend to $0$.

steps.slogan: Bound the cross term by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.
steps.detail: We have $\frac{1}{N+1}\sum_k |\alpha_k||\beta_{N-k}| \le \big(\frac{1}{N+1}\sum_k |\alpha_k|^2\big)^{1/2}\big(\frac{1}{N+1}\sum_k |\beta_k|^2\big)^{1/2}$. The sequences $|\alpha_k|^2$ and $|\beta_k|^2$ are null, so both factors tend to $0$ by the previous step.

steps.slogan: Combine the limits to get the Cesàro mean $AB$.
steps.detail: By the first two steps the means $\frac{1}{N+1}(C_0 + \dots + C_N)$ equal $AB$ plus three terms. The previous two steps show that these terms tend to $0$, so the means converge to $AB$.

concepts.c:series: The theorem concerns the partial sums of two series and their product series.
concepts.c:absolute-convergence: Absolute convergence is the stronger hypothesis of the related theorems.

source.note: Cesàro's theorem on the product of series (E. Cesàro, 1890) by the convolution of partial sums, as in G. H. Hardy, Divergent Series, Oxford University Press, 1949, on the multiplication of summable series.

statement: Let $B$ be a [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) on a module $M$ over a commutative ring, with finite [basis](c:basis) $b$. Let $c$ be another finite basis of $M$ and $P$ the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $c$ written in $b$. Then the matrix of $B$ in $c$ is $P^{\mathsf T}\,[B]_b\,P$.

hypotheses.text: The map $B\colon M \times M \to R$ is a [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) on a module over a commutative ring $R$.
The families $b$ and $c$ are finite [bases](c:basis) of $M$, and $P$ is the coordinate matrix of $c$ in $b$.

conclusion: $[B]_c = P^{\mathsf T}\,[B]_b\,P$, where $[B]_b$ has entries $B(b_i, b_j)$.

formal.difference: The declaration is more general: for linear maps $l, r$ from a module with basis $c$ into the module with basis $b$, the matrix of $B(l\,\cdot, r\,\cdot)$ in $c$ is $[l]^{\mathsf T}[B]_b[r]$. The change of basis is the case $l = r = \mathrm{id}$.

proofs.name: Entrywise expansion
proofs.slogan: Expand the new basis vectors in the old basis, use bilinearity in both arguments, and read the double sum as a matrix product.
proofs.scope: The change of basis on one module, with $l = r = \mathrm{id}$. The proof is the entrywise computation that gives the general declaration.

roles.why: Bilinearity lets $B$ be expanded in each argument separately.
The bases give coordinates, and the columns of $P$ expand $c$ in $b$.

steps.slogan: Write the matrix of $B$ in a basis through its values on basis vectors.
steps.detail: The matrix $[B]_c$ has entry $B(c_k, c_m)$ in row $k$ and column $m$, and $[B]_b$ has entry $B(b_i, b_j)$ in row $i$ and column $j$.

steps.slogan: Expand each new basis vector in the old basis.
steps.detail: By definition of $P$, the $k$-th column holds the $b$-coordinates of $c_k$, so $c_k = \sum_i P_{ik}\, b_i$ for every $k$.

steps.slogan: Expand $B(c_k, c_m)$ by bilinearity in both arguments.
steps.detail: Linearity in the first argument and then in the second gives $B(c_k, c_m) = \sum_{i,j} P_{ik}\, B(b_i, b_j)\, P_{jm}$.

steps.slogan: Recognize the double sum as an entry of a matrix product.
steps.detail: The sum equals $\sum_{i,j} (P^{\mathsf T})_{ki}\,[B]_b(i, j)\,P_{jm}$, which is the $(k, m)$ entry of $P^{\mathsf T}[B]_b P$. All entries agree, so $[B]_c = P^{\mathsf T}[B]_b P$.

concepts.c:bilinear-form: Bilinearity turns the values on new basis vectors into sums over old ones.
concepts.c:basis: A basis gives the coordinates that define both matrices and the matrix $P$.

source.note: mathlib proves BilinForm.toMatrix_comp from LinearMap.toMatrix₂_compl₁₂, the same entrywise expansion with the coordinate matrices of $l$ and $r$.

statement: Let $f\colon R \to S$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings of [finite presentation](c:finitely-presented-morphism) and $T$ a [constructible set](c:constructible-set) in the [prime spectrum](c:prime-spectrum) $\operatorname{Spec} S$. Then the image of $T$ under $\operatorname{Spec} f$ is constructible in $\operatorname{Spec} R$.

hypotheses.text: The ring map $f$ is of [finite presentation](c:finitely-presented-morphism).
The subset $T \subseteq \operatorname{Spec} S$ is a [constructible set](c:constructible-set).

conclusion: The image $\operatorname{Spec}(f)(T)$ is a constructible subset of $\operatorname{Spec} R$.

proofs.name: Induction on the presentation
proofs.slogan: Factor $f$ into polynomial extensions and a quotient by a finitely generated ideal, and prove the image statement for each factor.
proofs.scope: The affine statement for commutative rings. The scheme version for finitely presented quasi-compact quasi-separated morphisms follows by covering with affine opens, which is not proved here.

roles.why: A finite presentation factors $f$ through a polynomial ring and a quotient by a finitely generated ideal.
Constructible sets are finite unions of simple sets $V(g_1,\dots,g_k) \cap D(h)$ that the polynomial case handles.

steps.slogan: Factor $f$ into polynomial extensions followed by a surjection.
steps.detail: A presentation gives a surjection $R[X_1, \dots, X_n] \to S$ with finitely generated kernel $I$. Adjoining one variable at a time writes $f$ as a composite of maps $A \to A[X]$ followed by a surjection with finitely generated kernel. Images compose, so it is enough to treat these two kinds of map.

steps.slogan: Treat a surjection with finitely generated kernel.
steps.detail: For $A \to A/I$ with $I$ finitely generated, $\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)$ is the closed set $V(I)$, and its complement is a finite union of basic opens, hence quasi-compact. A constructible subset of $V(I)$ is then constructible in $\operatorname{Spec} A$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the case $A \to A[X]$ to the basic sets $V(g_1,\dots,g_k) \cap D(h)$.
steps.detail: A constructible set in $\operatorname{Spec} A[X]$ is a finite union of sets $V(g_1, \dots, g_k) \cap D(h)$. The image of a union is the union of the images. So it suffices to treat one such set, by induction on the number and the degrees of the $g_i$.

steps.slogan: Lower the degrees by splitting on a leading coefficient.
steps.detail: Let $a$ be the leading coefficient of $g_1$. Over $D(a)$ the polynomial $g_1$ has a unit leading coefficient, so division with remainder replaces $g_2, \dots, g_k$ and $h$ by remainders of lower degree. On $V(a)$, replace $g_1$ by $g_1 - aX^d$ and add $a$ as a constant polynomial. Each branch has smaller degree data.

steps.slogan: Settle the base cases explicitly.
steps.detail: With no $g_i$, the image of $D(h)$ is the union of the opens $D(h_j)$ over the coefficients $h_j$. With one monic $g_1$ of degree $d$, $A[X]/(g_1)$ is free of rank $d$, and a prime $\mathfrak p$ is in the image iff $h^d \not\equiv 0$ in $\kappa(\mathfrak p)[X]/(g_1)$. That is open: some coefficient of $h^d \bmod g_1$ lies outside $\mathfrak p$.

steps.slogan: Assemble the images along the factorization.
steps.detail: The previous steps give constructible images for $A \to A[X]$ and for surjections with finitely generated kernel. Following $R \to R[X_1] \to \cdots \to R[X_1, \dots, X_n] \to S$ and composing, the image of $T$ under $\operatorname{Spec} f$ is constructible.

concepts.c:finitely-presented-morphism: Finite presentation gives the factorization into polynomial maps and a finitely generated quotient.
concepts.c:constructible-set: Constructible sets are the class that stays closed under images.
concepts.c:prime-spectrum: The statement is about images of subsets of prime spectra under $\operatorname{Spec} f$.

statement: Let $G$ be an unambiguous [context-free grammar](c:context-free-language) and $a_n$ the number of words of length $n$ in its language. Then the [generating function](c:generating-function) $f(z) = \sum_n a_n z^n$ is algebraic: $P(z, f(z)) = 0$ for a nonzero polynomial $P$ with rational coefficients.

hypotheses.text: The grammar $G$ is a [context-free grammar](c:context-free-language) over a finite alphabet.
Every word of the language of $G$ has exactly one parse tree.

conclusion: The series $f(z)$ is a root of a nonzero polynomial in $\mathbb{Q}[z][y]$.

proofs.name: Algebraic system of equations
proofs.slogan: Turn unique parse trees into a polynomial system for the generating functions of the nonterminals, then show that the solution is algebraic by a differential argument.
proofs.scope: The grammar is first made proper, which keeps unambiguity and changes the language at most by the empty word. The empty word changes $f$ by the constant 1.

roles.why: The rules of the grammar give one monomial per production in the system of equations.
Unique parse trees make the generating function count words, not trees, and make the system exact.

steps.slogan: Reduce to a proper grammar without empty or unit rules.
steps.detail: Remove useless symbols, $\varepsilon$-rules and unit rules by the standard constructions. They give a bijection of parse trees, so the new grammar is unambiguous, and they change the language only by the empty word. Then every rule is a single terminal or has length at least 2.

steps.slogan: Write one equation for each nonterminal from the unique parse trees.
steps.detail: Let $y_i(z)$ be the generating function of words derived from the nonterminal $N_i$. A word derived from $N_i$ has one first rule $N_i \to \alpha$ and, for each nonterminal in $\alpha$, one subword with a unique tree. So $y_i = \sum_{N_i \to \alpha} z^{t(\alpha)} \prod_j y_j^{e_j(\alpha)} =: P_i(y, z)$, where $t(\alpha)$ counts the terminals of $\alpha$.

steps.slogan: Show that $I - \partial P/\partial y$ is invertible over the power series ring.
steps.detail: Each $y_j$ is a [formal power series](c:formal-power-series) without constant term, because words are nonempty. A rule of length at least 2 gives a monomial whose partial derivatives vanish at $z = 0$. So the [Jacobian matrix](c:jacobian-matrix) $\partial P/\partial y$ has entries without constant term, and $\det(I - \partial P/\partial y)$ has constant term 1.

steps.slogan: Show that every $y_i$ is algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}(z)$.
steps.detail: Let $K = \mathbb{Q}(z)(y_1, \dots, y_m)$. Differentiating $y_i = P_i(y, z)$ in the module of differentials $\Omega_{K/\mathbb{Q}(z)}$, with $dz = 0$, gives $(I - \partial P/\partial y)\,dy = 0$. The determinant is a nonzero element of $K$, so $dy_i = 0$. In characteristic 0, a finitely generated extension with $\Omega = 0$ has transcendence degree 0, so it is algebraic.

steps.slogan: Read off the generating function of the language.
steps.detail: The start symbol $S$ gives $f = y_S$, plus 1 if the empty word was removed. The elements algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}(z)$ form a field, so $f$ is a root of a nonzero polynomial $P(z, y)$ with rational coefficients.

concepts.c:context-free-language: Its grammar rules supply the monomials of the equation system.
concepts.c:generating-function: Counting words by length is done with a generating function.
concepts.c:formal-power-series: The generating functions are formal power series, with nonempty words giving no constant term.
concepts.c:jacobian-matrix: Invertibility of the Jacobian matrix forces the solution to be algebraic.

source.note: The enumeration theorem of N. Chomsky and M. P. Schützenberger, The algebraic theory of context-free languages, in Computer Programming and Formal Systems, North-Holland, 1963, pp. 118-161. The elimination step is replaced here by a differential argument.

statement: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a symmetric monoidal $(\infty, n)$-[category](c:infinity-n-category). Evaluation at the point is an equivalence from the space of symmetric monoidal functors $\mathrm{Bord}_n^{\mathrm{fr}} \to \mathcal{C}$ to the space of [fully dualizable](c:fully-dualizable-object) objects of $\mathcal{C}$.

hypotheses.text: The target $\mathcal{C}$ is a symmetric monoidal $(\infty, n)$-[category](c:infinity-n-category) for some $n \ge 0$.

conclusion: Framed $n$-dimensional [topological field theories](c:topological-quantum-field-theory) with values in $\mathcal{C}$ correspond to fully dualizable objects of $\mathcal{C}$, by evaluation at a point.

proofs.name: Framed bordisms and handles
proofs.slogan: Show that the point is fully dualizable, present framed bordisms by handles, and compare the bordism category with the free category on a fully dualizable object.
proofs.scope: The framed version for every $n \ge 0$; the proof here is an outline of Lurie's, and the steps on Morse theory and the induction rest on the cited work. Versions with other tangential structure follow by taking homotopy fixed points of the $O(n)$-action.

roles.why: The target is the higher category in which the images of the point and of the bordisms live.

steps.slogan: Formulate framed bordisms and full dualizability for $(\infty, n)$-categories.
steps.detail: Lurie models $(\infty, n)$-categories as complete $n$-fold Segal spaces and defines the symmetric monoidal $(\infty, n)$-category $\mathrm{Bord}_n^{\mathrm{fr}}$ of framed bordisms. A [fully dualizable](c:fully-dualizable-object) object has a dual and, recursively, adjoints for all its evaluation and coevaluation morphisms.

steps.slogan: Show that the point of $\mathrm{Bord}_n^{\mathrm{fr}}$ is fully dualizable.
steps.detail: Half-circles give evaluation and coevaluation for the point, and higher framed handles give the adjoints of these morphisms. A symmetric monoidal functor preserves duals and adjoints, so evaluation at the point sends a functor $\mathrm{Bord}_n^{\mathrm{fr}} \to \mathcal{C}$ to a fully dualizable object.

steps.slogan: Present framed bordisms by handles through Morse theory.
steps.detail: Every framed bordism has a framed generalized Morse function and so factors into elementary handle bordisms. Lurie's outline uses the connectivity of the space of framed functions (Igusa) to control the relations between two factorizations, namely handle cancellations and their higher coherences.

steps.slogan: Compare the bordism category with the free category by induction on $n$.
steps.detail: The handle presentation identifies $\mathrm{Bord}_n^{\mathrm{fr}}$ with the symmetric monoidal $(\infty, n)$-category freely generated by one object with duals and adjoints. Lurie organizes the comparison as an induction on $n$, passing to categories of morphisms of dimension $n - 1$.

steps.slogan: Read the equivalence as the classification of framed field theories.
steps.detail: Freeness says that functors out of $\mathrm{Bord}_n^{\mathrm{fr}}$ correspond to the choice of a fully dualizable object in the target. So evaluation at the point is an equivalence onto the space of fully dualizable objects, which classifies framed [topological field theories](c:topological-quantum-field-theory).

concepts.c:infinity-n-category: The target and the bordism category are both higher categories of this kind.
concepts.c:fully-dualizable-object: Full dualizability is the exact condition that the point satisfies and that classifies theories.
concepts.c:topological-quantum-field-theory: Framed topological field theories are the symmetric monoidal functors that the theorem classifies.

source.ref: J. Lurie, On the classification of topological field theories, Current Developments in Mathematics 2008, International Press, 2009, pp. 129-280
source.note: Lurie outlines the proof of the framed cobordism hypothesis (his Theorem 2.4.6). A second approach through the tangle hypothesis and factorization homology is D. Ayala and J. Francis, The cobordism hypothesis, arXiv:1705.02240, which assumes a conjecture on factorization homology with adjoints.
